title: TS SDK streaming adapter: single-entry conversion utilities + ergonomic examples
creator: Sofia Chen
description:
Problem: Our TypeScript SDK currently exposes multiple fragmented helpers for streaming (separate adapters for AsyncIterator -> ReadableStream, and ad-hoc examples for ReadableStream -> AsyncIterator). This causes confusion for integrators trying to wire streaming responses into browser APIs, Node stream ecosystems, or server frameworks. We also lack clear semantics for cancellation propagation, backpressure, text decoding, chunk coalescing, and resume/retry of interrupted streaming responses.

Goal: Deliver a single, well-documented, type-safe utilities module that provides canonical conversions between AsyncIterable<T> and Web ReadableStream (and a small set of ergonomic examples for common patterns). Ship tests, examples for Node/browser, and a short guide that shows how to implement retries that reconnect and resume tokenized streams when partial responses are available.

Scope / deliverables:
- Implement two primary exported helpers: "streamFromAsyncIterator" and "asyncIteratorFromStream" with consistent TypeScript generics (T = string | Uint8Array | TokenChunk).
- Provide an optional "duplex" helper that returns an object with both an AsyncIterator input sink and a ReadableStream output to simplify bridge scenarios (client-side fetch + service worker, serverless adapters).
- Ensure AbortSignal/AbortController cancellation propagates both directions. If the ReadableStream consumer calls cancel(), the underlying AsyncIterator should receive a well-documented signal to cleanup; if the iterator throws a CancelledError, the stream should close gracefully.
- Backpressure semantics: implement chunk queueing bound by a configurable maxBufferedBytes / maxBufferedChunks option and expose a policy that prefers rounding to line breaks for text streams. Provide safe defaults for browser and Node usage.
- Retry and resume example: a canonical example that shows how to reconnect using a continuation token or a token-offset heuristic; demonstrate how to emit a special "RESUME_BOUNDARY" marker so downstream consumers can stitch pieces with minimal duplication.
- Examples and tests: browser example (fetch + ReadableStream consumer), Node example (Readable.from + transform pipeline), and an end-to-end test that simulates transient network failures and verifies no token loss when using the resume helper.
- Docs: small guide in the SDK docs site with copy-paste snippets and a migration note for existing helpers.

Non-goals: full-blown remapping of existing SDK API shapes, implementing server-side protocol-level resume (we'll provide patterns instead), polyfilling old Node versions beyond LTS-18.

Trade-offs considered:
- Using a single, opinionated adapter reduces cognitive load but requires careful choice of defaults (buffer sizes, text decoder options). We prefer explicit opt-ins for aggressive buffering or lossy coalescing.
- Resume heuristics are application-specific; we will provide a small, well-tested pattern rather than trying to generalize every use case.

Acceptance criteria (high-level):
- Unit tests covering cancellation, backpressure, and basic conversion semantics (100% for adapter module).
- Integration test that runs the browser example in Playwright or a headless Node simulation.
- API exported from @redwood/sdk/streams (or similar) and documented in the TS SDK docs with at least 3 examples.
- PR with implementation, tests, docs and at least two engineering reviewers sign-off.
acceptance_criteria: streamFromAsyncIterator and asyncIteratorFromStream exported with clear generics
AbortSignal cancellation propagates both ways and is covered by tests
Backpressure and bounded buffer parameters configurable and tested
Retry/resume example demonstrates reconnect + stitch without token duplication
Documentation and three runnable examples (browser, node, e2e simulation)
Two code reviewers have approved the PR
